clue.text: This Jane film was a hit in London

definitions.text: This Jane film was a hit in London

parts.words: This Jane film was a hit in London
parts.note: the clue points to the Doris Day Western named after a frontierswoman called Jane, whose first name also means a disaster or heavy blow

explanation.surface: A remark that a film about a woman called Jane did well at the London box office.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1953 musical Western is named after the frontierswoman Martha Jane Canary, nicknamed for her habit of attracting trouble; 'a hit' hints at the other sense, a misfortune that strikes.
explanation.definitionFit: The frontierswoman's nickname is the ordinary word for a disaster, and the film bearing it was a box-office success.

clue.text: Small bottle for sprinkling oil perhaps

definitions.meaning: a little cruet with holes in its lid for shaking out sugar or salt
the seed oil long used as a purgative, here given as one example of an oil

explanation.surface: A tiny flask used for sprinkling oil over food.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs the bottle and the oil; they are two separate senses of one word, the second taken from the name of the oil.
explanation.definitionFit: A small pot with a perforated top for shaking sugar or pepper, and the oil pressed from the beans of a tropical plant used as a laxative.

clue.text: Longitude measured after sudden landfall

definitions.meaning: in an old sense longitude means extent from end to end, long measurement
someone who falls flat is said to measure their ... on the ground

explanation.surface: A ship's position in longitude is worked out after an unexpected sighting of land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'landfall' suggests a ship sighting the coast; it is a person suddenly hitting the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for longitudinal extent, and the idiom 'to measure one's length', meaning to fall flat on the ground.

clue.text: Scotsman in the bilge needs an oilskin

parts.note: Mac, the prefix of many Scottish surnames, stands for a Scotsman
bilge is nonsense, and so is tosh

explanation.surface: A Scottish sailor down in the ship's bilge needs his waterproof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bilge' looks nautical, which suits the oilskin; here it means rubbish talk, TOSH. 'needs' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubberised raincoat, named after its Scottish inventor, is a waterproof coat like a sailor's oilskin.

clue.text: Dig out the best suit and succeed unexpectedly

definitions.meaning: at cards, to expose cards of the suit that beats all others
the idiom for coming good when least expected

explanation.surface: Someone finds their smartest outfit at the back of the wardrobe and wins a surprise triumph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'best suit' suggests clothes; it is the ruling suit in a card game.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally to reveal cards of the winning suit at bridge or whist, and idiomatically to do far better than expected.

clue.text: Does a funny thing when about to meditate

parts.note: a. is a standard abbreviation for about, approximately
to muse is to meditate or ponder, so he muses

explanation.surface: Someone performs a comic act while on the point of quiet contemplation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when' is only a link; 'about' gives the single letter A, the abbreviation for 'about' in dates and measurements.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain someone with a joke or comic act is what doing something funny for them achieves.

clue.text: Choral piece for putting totem up the pole

indicators.note: up the pole is British slang for crazy, so the letters of totem are sent haywire

explanation.surface: A song sung while a totem is raised to the top of its pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up the pole' looks literal, but in British slang it means mad, signalling a jumble of TOTEM; 'for putting' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A polyphonic sacred composition for unaccompanied voices is a piece for a choir.

clue.text: Robespierre's deep colour

definitions.note: an adjective standing for Robespierre, whom Carlyle called the sea-hued Incorruptible

parts.note: the deep is a poetic name for the ocean
green is a colour

explanation.surface: The French revolutionary's favourite rich shade.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Carlyle's history of the French Revolution nicknamed Robespierre 'the Incorruptible' with this colour, supposedly from his complexion.
explanation.definitionFit: Carlyle's epithet for the Jacobin leader made this bluish-green tint his signature, so the colour is Robespierre's own.

clue.text: Where to detain a slippery customer while bathing

definitions.text: Where to detain a slippery customer while bathing

parts.words: Where to detain a slippery customer while bathing
parts.note: the slippery customer sounds like a crook but is the bar you lather with, held in a tray beside the bath

explanation.walkthrough: 'detain' and 'slippery customer' suggest police and a fugitive; the escapee is a wet bar of cleanser.
explanation.definitionFit: A shallow tray by the bath holds the bar of cleanser so it does not slide away.

clue.text: Duty-free post

parts.note: read not as tax-free shopping but as a job that carries no duties at all

explanation.walkthrough: 'Duty-free' suggests customs and airport shops; here it means free of work, a paid position with no real responsibilities.
explanation.definitionFit: A cushy office paying a salary while requiring little or no work is exactly a job without duties.

clue.text: A pie's rising in layers

indicators.note: in this clue rising tells us to read the words A pie's from the end back to the start

parts.note: a tart is a pie, and the 's makes it plural-looking: tarts

explanation.surface: Pastry puffing up in the oven, rising in flaky layers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns the whole of A TARTS around, giving the run of letters backwards; 'in' is a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Geologists call bands of rock laid one upon another by this Latin plural, meaning layers or levels.

clue.text: They say Jim has this twin rail set

definitions.meaning: Jim heard aloud is gym, and a gymnasium is equipped with this apparatus
a set of two matching rails, as in the men's gymnastics event

explanation.surface: Gossip that a man called Jim owns a model railway with two tracks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jim' is a man's name heard as gym; 'twin rail set' suggests a toy train set.
explanation.definitionFit: Gymnastic apparatus of two raised horizontal rails side by side, found in any gym, which sounds like Jim.

clue.text: Contributor to have a go at ending of serial, say

indicators.note: the words that follow each contribute some letters, and together they have the answer held within them

explanation.surface: A writer contributing to a magazine is about to attempt the final episode of a serialised story.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside 'go at ending'. 'Serial, say' is read as a sound-alike for cereal, so the definition means 'of cereal'; oats are a cereal.
explanation.definitionFit: Made of oats, a cereal grain, as in oatmeal porridge or a shepherd's pipe of oat straw.

clue.text: Having no change, and the rental due for revision!

indicators.note: revision means altering, so the letters of rental and due are to be altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A tenant pays the same as before, though the rent is supposedly due to be reviewed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for revision' asks for the nine letters of RENTAL DUE to be rearranged; 'and the' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Something left as it was, unmodified, has undergone no change.

clue.text: Opposition against State head

parts.note: contra is Latin for against, as in pro and contra
RI is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Rhode Island
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Sheerness

explanation.surface: A protest against the leader of a country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' is a geographical headland, not a leader: a NESS, as in many British place names.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit of perverse opposition, always taking the other side, is what being difficult and obstinate amounts to.

clue.text: He uses a couple of blades for the fish in the freezer

definitions.text: He uses a couple of blades

indicators.note: in says the word for fish is placed inside the word for freezer

parts.note: an icer is something that ices or freezes
a skate is a flat ray-like fish

explanation.surface: A fishmonger uses two knives to deal with fish taken from the freezer.
explanation.walkthrough: The page has no stray stops after 'He' or before 'the'. 'blades' are not knives but the runners on two boots; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A person gliding on a rink wears boots with a pair of metal runners, one under each foot.

clue.text: Paul's car is broken down on the shoulder

indicators.note: a car that has broken down is out of order, so these letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: Paul's car has broken down and sits on the hard shoulder of the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken down' rearranges the letters of PAULS CAR; 'is' is a link. The shoulder looks like a motorway verge but is the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: An anatomical adjective for the shoulder blade, also a monk's garment worn over the shoulders.

clue.text: River I fish in sleeved jacket

parts.note: the Cam is the river flowing through Cambridge
the sole is a flatfish

explanation.surface: An angler on a river catching fish while wearing a jacket with sleeves.
explanation.walkthrough: The garment's older sense was a short sleeved jacket, not today's sleeveless top; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically the word named a woman's short sleeved jacket or bodice before it came to mean a strappy undergarment.

clue.text: Victoria Mason works in the body shop

definitions.note: read as one who works in the body shop: the definition describes the person's trade

parts.note: a victoria is a light four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage, a kind of coach
a mason is a builder in stone

explanation.surface: A man named Victoria Mason has a job in a car repair garage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victoria Mason' looks like a person's name; it is a carriage and a stonemason. The body shop is where vehicle bodies are made.
explanation.definitionFit: A craftsman who makes the bodywork of vehicles, once carriages and now cars, works where bodies are built.

clue.text: Eastern bird out of holy writ, of course

parts.note: NT, the New Testament, is a book taken out of holy writ
a ree or reeve is the female ruff, a wading bird

explanation.surface: An Oriental bird released from sacred scripture, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads like 'naturally'; the definition is 'course', a dish in a meal, with 'of' as link. The bird's letters go after the scripture abbreviation they come out of.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish served between the fish and the main roast, or in America the main dish itself, is a stage of the meal.

clue.text: Cavalry officer's business runs free of tax

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a business
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
a net sum is what remains after deductions such as tax

explanation.surface: A cavalry officer's company earns profits without paying tax.
explanation.walkthrough: In the old British cavalry the lowest commissioned officer, who carried the troop's colours, held this rank.
explanation.definitionFit: The fifth grade of commissioned officer in a cavalry troop, equivalent to an ensign, held this title.

clue.text: Rule announced by the head

indicators.note: announced means spoken out loud, so the word for rule is heard rather than seen

parts.note: a principle is a rule or law guiding conduct

explanation.surface: A regulation proclaimed by the headmaster at assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: The two spellings sound alike: the rule is spelt -PLE, the head of a college -PAL.
explanation.definitionFit: The chief of a school or college is called by this title, the person in charge.

clue.text: Demand seafood about one

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the shellfish goes round the word for one

parts.note: a clam is a shellfish eaten as seafood
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Insisting on shellfish for a single diner.
explanation.definitionFit: To assert a right to something is to insist on having it.

clue.text: Lad to deal with fencing in the East

parts.note: Ken is a common boy's name
to do a task is to deal with it

explanation.surface: A boy tasked with putting up fences somewhere in eastern parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fencing' looks like erecting fences; it is the sport, and 'in the East' places it in Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese martial art of swordsmanship with bamboo staves is Oriental sword-fighting.

clue.text: Lavatory, note, needs washer

parts.note: loo is British slang for a lavatory or toilet
fah is the fourth note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A complaint that the toilet needs a new washer, as a plumber's note might say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'washer' suggests a plumbing part; it is something you wash with, a dried gourd used as a bath sponge.
explanation.definitionFit: The fibrous dried pod of a tropical gourd is used as a scrubbing sponge, a thing to wash with.

clue.text: Found goose very hard

parts.note: to found metal is to cast it in a mould, as in a foundry
a goose is a tailor's heavy smoothing iron, named for its curved handle

explanation.surface: Someone discovers that a goose is extremely tough to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' is not the past of find but the verb of the foundry; 'goose' is not the bird but a tailor's pressing iron.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal poured into moulds becomes rigid and brittle, so the phrase means unbreakably firm, as in a watertight alibi.

clue.text: Broad sounds full of water here

indicators.note: sounds says the word for broad must be heard, not read as written

parts.note: roomy means spacious or broad

explanation.surface: A wide stretch of the Norfolk Broads, with its waterways, described as full of water here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broad' tempts as the Norfolk Broads, lakes in eastern England; it means spacious. 'here' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyes that stream with watery discharge, as in old age or with a cold, are described with this adjective.

clue.text: Tureen is prepared for the greedy

indicators.note: a dish that is prepared is made up, so the letters are made up into something new

explanation.surface: A soup tureen is made ready for gluttonous diners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prepared' rearranges the eight letters of TUREEN IS; 'for the' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary word for hungry and greedy, from the Latin for wanting to eat.
